item.title: The Opener: Ramirez, Taylor, MLB Proposal
item.dc:creator: Charlie Wright
item.description: The streak continues. The White Sox whiffed on both chances to clinch a series at home for the first time since 1906. Sam Antonacci ...
item.content:encoded:
The streak continues. The White Sox whiffed on both chances to clinch a series at home for the first time since 1906. Sam Antonacci isn’t worried about bouncing back in Game 5, though. “I got asked that yesterday. I said we’d turn the page today. We turned the page but we lost so we’ll turn 3 pages and hopefully win on Saturday.” (h/t Jesse Rogers of ESPN)

1. Ramirez heating up at the right time

Jose Ramirez’s lingering hand issue has been a key storyline for the Guardians down the stretch. The seven-time All-Star returned from a fractured hamate bone in late July. Ramirez posted a .598 OPS with just two homers in 53 games to close the regular season. He went 0-for-6 with three strikeouts in the first two games of the ALDS (both losses), but has come alive lately. Ramirez drilled a two-run homer to give Cleveland its first lead in Game 4. He finished with two hits and three RBI. Ramirez has four hits, five RBI, and four runs scored across Games 3 and 4.

2. Taylor falters in disastrous sixth inning

Versatile reliever Grant Taylor hadn’t allowed an earned run over his first 7 2/3 playoff innings, piling up 11 strikeouts and two saves. Manager Will Venable called on Taylor to put out a fire in the sixth inning with the go-ahead run at second base. He did the opposite. Taylor allowed six straight hitters to reach base, turning a tie game into a five-run deficit. Chicago made some noise in the ninth inning but ultimately came up short. They’ll head back to Cleveland for Game 5 on Saturday, and Taylor said he’ll be available. “If they want me to go 9, then go for it,” Taylor said (h/t Scott Merkin of MLB.com). “I’m going to do everything in the next couple of days to be ready to go.”

3. More details on MLB’s recent proposal

Major League Baseball shared details yesterday of a proposal to MLBPA that included a shorter season and tweaks to the playoff format. We covered the main points here, but a handful of other details emerged later in the day. The 154-game schedule would include Monday being a standard off-day for most teams, relays Rogers. The only Monday games would be national broadcasts or holiday-related slates. Memorial Day comes to mind as a Monday that would probably have a larger schedule of games. Evan Drellich of The Athletic pointed out that the league’s proposed schedule changes, set to begin in 2029, may be tied to TV deals. New national broadcast contracts are expected to start that year.

Photo courtesy of David Banks, Imagn Images

item.title: MLB Proposes Shorter Regular Season, Playoff Changes
item.dc:creator: Charlie Wright
item.description: Major League Baseball proposed a 154-game regular season during a collective bargaining session with the MLBPA today, per an announcement on X. The league ...
item.content:encoded:
Major League Baseball proposed a 154-game regular season during a collective bargaining session with the MLBPA today, per an announcement on X. The league also proposed changes to the postseason that would include extending the Division Series to seven games and allowing higher seeds to choose their opponents.

The current 162-game schedule was fully adopted in 1962. The regular season had previously been 154 games, hence the league’s phrasing of a return to that length. The MLB announcement mentions the institution of a “standard weekly off day benefiting player health” under the 154-game schedule.

Cutting eight games from the regular season dovetails with the increase in Division Series games. Expanding that round from a five-game set to a seven-game series would mean a maximum of eight extra playoff games. These two changes would take place in 2029, per the league proposal.

In a follow-up post on X, the league notes that the longer playoff series made possible by the shorter regular season would add extra off-days to the postseason schedule. This would give pitchers extra rest and limit the number of weekday daytime playoff games, argues the league.

“A shorter regular season unlocks making October even better for our fans—with fewer weekday afternoon games, a longer Division Series, and more opportunities to see the game’s best pitchers on the biggest stage,” MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said, relayed by Bob Nightengale of USA Today.

The playoff opponent selection would take place in the Wild Card and Division Series rounds, per the league’s proposal. In the first round, the No. 3 seed could choose between playing the No. 5 seed or the No. 6 seed. In the Division Series, the top seed would get to pick which of the Wild Card round winners it wanted to face. If accepted, the change would go into place for the 2027 season.

The setup would’ve made for some interesting decisions this postseason. Instead of playing the White Sox, the No. 3 Astros could’ve chosen to face the Red Sox. After the Braves and Padres advanced in the Wild Card round, the top-seeded Brewers could’ve opted to face Atlanta instead of San Diego.

The league’s scheduling proposals remain contingent on instituting the salary cap/floor system, as noted in their announcement. That’s been the main sticking point between the two sides. With the salary cap stipulation attached, it’s unlikely the MLBPA would accept the proposals. The union responded with a statement on X sharing that sentiment.

“Players will weigh in on these proposals and we will respond at the bargaining table,” the statement read in part. “Unfortunately, the league once again made it clear that all of its proposals are contingent on players’ agreement to a salary cap, a system that guts player rights and compensation.”

Photo courtesy of Brett Davis, Imagn Images

item.title: Jazz Chisholm Jr. Wants To Stay With Yankees
item.dc:creator: Connor Byrne
item.description: Despite going without superstar right fielder Aaron Judge for most of the season, the Yankees won 93 games and earned a playoff berth. They ...
item.content:encoded:
Despite going without superstar right fielder Aaron Judge for most of the season, the Yankees won 93 games and earned a playoff berth. They swept the archrival Red Sox in the Wild Card round, but the Yankees were then the victims of a sweep against another AL East foe – the division champion Rays – in the ALDS.  The Yankees are now turning their full attention to offseason matters, including whether to retain impending free agent second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. 

Chisholm, an All-Star for the second time in 2025, endured a down year at the plate and struggled both offensively and defensively in four appearances in the playoffs. Manager Aaron Boone left Chisholm out of the Yankees’ starting lineup for two postseason games, including their season-ending loss on Wednesday. The fans at Yankee Stadium booed Chisholm after he fouled out to first base as a pinch hitter in the bottom of the seventh inning. Nevertheless, Chisholm would rather continue his career with the Yankees than exit in free agency.

“I do hope to be back,” Chisholm said (via Brendan Kuty of The Athletic).

Regardless of whether he gets his wish, Chisholm may not sign for as much money as he expected entering the season. After Chisholm homered 30 times and stole 31 bases in 2025, he had visions of a 50-50 campaign dancing in his head when he reported to Spring Training in February. The 50-50 club consists of one player, Shohei Ohtani, who accomplished that mammoth feat two years ago. Chisholm did not come close to joining him in 2026.

While Chisholm stole a career-high 41 bases, his homer total dropped to 19 over 532 plate appearances. Chisholm’s overall line, which checked in at .242/.332/.481 last year, slid to .231/.312/.399. His production was 25% better than league average in 2025, per wRC+, but 2% below the mean this year. The lefty-swinging Chisholm continued to have a tough time versus same-handed pitchers, who have held him to an 82 wRC+ during his career. He has been much better when facing righties, though his 107 wRC+ against them this season still came in well below his lifetime mark (118).

Chisholm may have been fortunate just to register the middling numbers he put up in 2026, as his expected weighted on-base average (.294) was 18 points below his real wOBA (.312). He ranked in the league’s 16th percentile in xwOBA, and it was a similar story in expected batting average (.216; seventh percentile) and expected slugging percentage (.366; 24th percentile). Chisholm was also near the bottom of the league in K percentage (29.5; ninth percentile), though strikeouts have been part of the package since he debuted with the Marlins in 2020.

Turning to his work at the keystone, Chisholm made a couple of defensive miscues in the ALDS after drawing mixed reviews during the season. He was credited with minus-6 Defensive Runs Saved, which was the former outfielder’s first time finishing negatively in that metric as a second baseman. On the other hand, Outs Above Average (13) and Fielding Run Value (8) each liked Chisholm, who has typically garnered favorable marks in those categories. Among second basemen, only Cardinals NL Rookie of the Year contender JJ Wetherholt outdid Chisholm in OAA.

Regardless of position, the soon-to-be 29-year-old Chisholm will be one of the most established free agent hitters available if he visits the open market. Brandon Lowe (Pirates), Luis Arraez (Phillies) and former Yankee Gleyber Torres (Tigers) are also among unsigned second basemen for 2027. Chisholm and Lowe are the only members of that quartet eligible to receive the $23.15MM qualifying offer. In the Yankees’ case, it is “highly unlikely” they will extend the offer to Chisholm, according to Kuty. The Yankees did it last offseason for center fielder Trent Grisham, who was coming off a career year at the time, and it went down as a poor use of money. He accepted the $22.05MM offer and proceeded to trudge through a subpar, injury-shortened season.

Grisham seems certain to leave the Bronx in free agency this time around, and if Chisholm joins him, the Yankees will have to find someone else to man second. Luis García Jr., who could move off first base, as well as Anthony Volpe and José Caballero represent a few in-house possibilities.

Photo courtesy of Vincent Carchietta, Imagn Images (via Reuters Connect)

item.title: Michael King Open To Returning To Padres
item.dc:creator: Charlie Wright
item.description: The Padres were dispatched by the Brewers in the NLDS, despite the efforts of Michael King. The right-hander tossed five innings of one-run ball ...
item.content:encoded:
The Padres were dispatched by the Brewers in the NLDS, despite the efforts of Michael King. The right-hander tossed five innings of one-run ball in Game 2. He came back two days later and picked up a two-inning save in Game 3. He was supposedly available in Game 4, too.

King will be a key domino for San Diego this offseason. He holds a $28MM player option for the 2027 campaign. If he opts out, he’ll be owed a $5MM buyout. King also has a $30MM player option for 2028. After Wednesday’s loss, the veteran right-hander discussed his looming decision.

“San Diego’s been—been incredible for me, and it’s all the way across the country from home,” King told reporters, including Jeff Sanders of the San Diego Union-Tribune. “But now I feel like I have a—a second home on the West Coast, so it’s been awesome. And yeah, I hope to—hope to continue.”

Lingering health questions following an abbreviated 2025 season shaped King’s venture into free agency. He ultimately re-signed with the Padres after rejecting their qualifying offer. King was able to secure a deal that gave him a safety net if injuries struck again this year, along with the flexibility to pursue a longer-term contract if he remained healthy.

King delivered the biggest workload of his career in 2026. He set career highs in starts (32) and innings pitched (185). The righty tacked on 14 more frames in the playoffs. King provided stability to a staff crushed by injuries and poor performance this season. San Diego had to lean heavily on its elite bullpen due to question marks in the rotation. King was the only starter to complete five innings during the team’s playoff run.

While the volume was strong, King’s production fell off in multiple areas. His strikeout rate tumbled to 21%, while his walk rate rose to 9.2%. His swinging-strike rate dropped to 10.2%. King managed a 3.21 ERA in large part due to a .259 BABIP and a left-on-base rate above 80%. His xERA, xFIP, and SIERA were all between 4.30 and 4.40.

King is entering his age-32 season. He ranked seventh in the final edition of our Free Agent Power Rankings. He’s the fourth pitcher on the board, behind Tarik Skubal, Trevor Rogers, and Freddy Peralta. There’s a solid chance King could improve on the three-year, $75MM commitment he received from the Padres in his most recent trip through free agency. He proved his health this season and won’t have the qualifying offer attached to him this time around.

An opt-out seems like the most likely scenario, but that doesn’t mean King won’t end up back in San Diego. The Padres could re-sign him once again on a reworked agreement. Bringing King back would be a huge boost to an uncertain 2027 rotation. Walker Buehler and trade deadline acquisition Robbie Ray are both free agents. Griffin Canning and Lucas Giolito have mutual options that are unlikely to be picked up by the team. Joe Musgrove returned in the playoffs after missing each of the last two regular seasons. It’s a unit that will need plenty of work this offseason.
